question: Which country operates the NAVSTAR GPS?
explanation: GPS is American, GLONASS Russian, Galileo European and BeiDou (Compass) Chinese.

question: What is the main reason Europe developed Galileo?

options.text: To provide a back-up for VOR and DME
Because GPS cannot be used by civil aircraft
Because GPS does not cover Europe
To have a system under European control

explanation: Full access to GPS and GLONASS is controlled by other states, so Galileo gives Europe its own independent system for security reasons.

question: What is EGNOS?

options.text: A ground-based landing system at airports

explanation: EGNOS (European Geostationary Navigation Overlay Service) is a wide-area differential (SBAS) system adding integrity and accuracy to GPS.

question: What does a local-area differential GNSS (GBAS) mainly provide?

options.text: Accuracy and integrity for airfield approaches
A back-up to the aircraft's IRS
Communication with ATC by data link on the ground and in flight

explanation: Local-area differential GNSS corrects errors and monitors integrity near one aerodrome, for precision approaches.

question: What is a satellite's ephemeris?
explanation: Using Kepler's laws and a starting point, each satellite (space vehicle, SV) calculates its position throughout its orbit; this is its ephemeris.

question: What coordinate system do GNSS systems use for position?

options.text: Range and bearing from a ground station
Latitude and longitude on a flat chart
Grid coordinates on the UK Ordnance Survey

explanation: Positions are computed in an earth-referenced Cartesian system with its origin at the earth's centre, then converted to latitude, longitude and height.

question: Which earth model does GPS use, and which is the aviation standard?

options.text: PZ-90 for GPS; WGS-84 for aviation
WGS-84 for GPS; ED-50 for aviation

explanation: GPS uses WGS-84, which is also the international aviation standard. GLONASS uses PZ-90 and Galileo ETRS-89; conversion between them is a simple calculation.

question: Which earth model does GLONASS use?
explanation: GLONASS uses Parameters of the Earth 1990 (PZ-90). Combined GPS/GLONASS receivers must convert to a common model.

question: Why can't GNSS height be used on its own for vertical navigation near the ground?

options.text: GNSS gives no height information at all
GNSS height is always pressure altitude
The satellites are too high to measure height
The ellipsoid and sea level differ by tens of metres

explanation: The WGS-84 ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical shape; mean sea level (the geoid) departs from it by up to tens of metres. Without correction (as in GBAS), GNSS height is unsuitable for vertical guidance near the ground.

question: What are the three segments of GPS?
explanation: The space segment is the satellites; the control segment the master station and monitors; the user segment all the receivers.

question: From when is GPS time counted?

options.text: The time the receiver was switched on

explanation: GPS time runs in weeks and seconds from 6 January 1980. After 1 024 weeks (an epoch) the week count restarts at zero.

question: Why is a GPS-to-UTC correction included in the satellite broadcast?

options.text: GPS time runs faster than UTC by 1% each day
Each satellite runs its own time zone
GPS time is not adjusted for leap seconds
UTC is measured in weeks, not days

explanation: GPS time is referenced to UTC but is not kept in step with it (it ignores leap seconds), so the offset is broadcast.

question: How many satellites does the specified GPS operational constellation contain?
explanation: The specification is 24 SVs, though more (around 31) are normally operating.

question: At about what height do GPS satellites orbit?
explanation: GPS orbits are about 20 200 km high. 35 800 km is geostationary height; 19 100 km is GLONASS.

question: What is the orbital period of a GPS satellite?
explanation: GPS satellites complete an orbit in about 12 hours (11 h 58 min). GLONASS takes 11 h 15 min.

question: At what inclination are GPS orbital planes?
explanation: GPS uses six planes at 55°, equally spaced round the equator. GLONASS uses 65°, Galileo 56°.

question: How many GPS satellites will normally be in view above 5° elevation?
explanation: Satellite spacing gives an observer on or near the surface five to eight SVs at least 5° above the horizon.

question: What is the mask angle for GPS satellites?
explanation: A satellite below 5° elevation is masked — not used — because its signal passes through a lot of atmosphere and is prone to errors.

question: What kind of clocks do GPS satellites carry?

options.text: A clock reset from the ground every minute
Several caesium or rubidium atomic clocks
A clock synchronised to the receiver

explanation: Each SV has 3 or 4 atomic clocks, accurate to about 1 nanosecond.

question: What frequency is GPS L1?
explanation: L1 is 1 575.42 MHz, carrying the C/A code, the P code and the navigation message. L2 (1 227.6 MHz) carries the P code.

question: Which GPS code is available to civil users?
explanation: Civil users have the C/A code. The P code (encrypted as Y code with anti-spoofing) is for military and authorised users.

question: How often does the GPS C/A code repeat?
explanation: The C/A code (1.023 MHz) repeats every millisecond; the P code (10.23 MHz) repeats every seven days.

question: At what rate is the GPS navigation message sent?
explanation: The navigation and system data message is sent at 50 bps and used with both codes.

question: Why does GPS transmit on two frequencies?

options.text: To double the number of satellites
To measure and remove ionospheric delay
To separate civil and military users by distance

explanation: Ionospheric delay depends on frequency. Comparing arrival times on two frequencies lets the receiver work out the delay.

question: What two functions do the PRN codes perform?

options.text: Satellite power control and range timing

explanation: Each SV has its own pseudo-random noise code, which identifies it and lets the receiver measure the signal's travel time.

question: Which item is in the GPS navigation message?
explanation: The message contains SV position, SV clock time and error, ionospheric data, the almanac, SV health and GPS-UTC correlation.

question: Which service uses the C/A code only?
explanation: SPS uses C/A; PPS uses both C/A and P codes.

question: How does GLONASS distinguish its satellites, unlike GPS?

options.text: Each transmits at a different time
Each uses a different code on the same frequency
Each uses a different frequency with the same code

explanation: GPS gives each SV its own code on common frequencies; GLONASS gives all SVs the same codes on different frequencies.

question: How many orbital planes does GLONASS use?
explanation: GLONASS has 24 SVs in three planes inclined at 65°, orbit 19 100 km, period 11 h 15 min.

question: What is Galileo's approximate orbital height?
explanation: Galileo uses about 30 SVs in three planes at 56°, about 23 222 km high, with a period of about 14 h 7 min.

question: What was the US Transit system?

options.text: An early satellite navigation system from the 1950s–60s
The current US satellite augmentation system

explanation: Space-based navigation began with Transit. The current generation of systems began development in the 1970s.

question: How long does the GPS P code take to repeat?
explanation: The P code (10.23 MHz) repeats every seven days; the C/A code every millisecond.

question: What is the P code called when anti-spoofing is applied?
explanation: With anti-spoofing the P code is encrypted as the Y code, usable only with the decryption keys.

question: What does the GPS control segment consist of?

options.text: A ground transmitter and monitor at each international airport
Master and back-up stations, and monitors

explanation: The control segment is a master control station, a back-up station and monitoring stations around the world.

question: How often do the monitor stations check each satellite's position and clock?
explanation: Errors build up because of the sun, moon, planets and solar radiation, so SV position and clock are checked at least every 12 hours.

question: When the control segment finds a satellite clock error, what happens?

options.text: It is broadcast by the satellite for correction
The receivers must be reset by the pilot
The satellite clock is reset immediately from the ground station

explanation: SV clocks cannot be adjusted, so the error is broadcast for receivers to correct. Position errors are sent to the SV to update its ephemeris.

question: Which type of GPS receiver is preferred for aviation?

options.text: Sequential, scanning one satellite at a time

explanation: Multi-channel (all-in-view) receivers track many SVs at once and pick the best four, giving instant position.

question: How long does a GPS navigation message frame take to receive?
explanation: One frame of 5 subframes, each 6 seconds, takes 30 seconds.

question: How long does it take to download the whole GPS almanac?
explanation: The almanac needs 25 frames at 30 s each: 12.5 minutes.

question: What is the almanac used for?

options.text: Predicting which satellites are in view
Correcting the receiver's clock to within one nanosecond

explanation: With a valid almanac and roughly known position and time, the receiver knows which SVs to look for and can start fixing quickly.

question: If the almanac is lost, about how long will the time to first fix be?
explanation: Downloading the almanac takes 12.5 minutes and the sky search at least 2.5 more. With a valid almanac, first fix takes about 30 seconds.

question: How does a GPS receiver measure the time a signal took to arrive?

options.text: By aligning its own copy of the PRN code
By measuring the Doppler shift of the carrier
By sending a pulse to the satellite and timing the reply
By comparing the phase of two 30 Hz tones

explanation: The receiver generates the same code and shifts it until it lines up with the received code; the shift is the travel time.

question: Why is the first range measurement called a pseudo-range?

options.text: It is the range to the earth's centre
It is a two-way range divided by two
It is measured to the wrong satellite
It still includes the receiver's clock error

explanation: The receiver's quartz clock is far less accurate than the SVs' atomic clocks, so each measured range includes the clock error until it is solved for.

question: A receiver clock is 1 ms fast. By about how much will each pseudo-range be in error?
explanation: Radio waves travel 162 000 NM per second, so 0.001 s = 162 NM. The receiver clock is kept deliberately in error one way so corrections always go in the same direction.

question: Why does a GPS receiver need four satellites for a 3D fix?

options.text: Because each satellite gives only one coordinate
Because one satellite is always a spare
To solve for X, Y, Z and the receiver clock error
To give one satellite for each quadrant

explanation: Four unknowns (X, Y, Z and time) need four equations. Four SVs give a 3D position and accurate time — a 4D fix.

question: With only three satellites, how can a receiver still produce a 3D position?

options.text: It cannot; it reverts to dead reckoning
By using a satellite below the mask angle
By using an input of altitude

explanation: Altitude acts like a fourth SV at the earth's centre. The position is less accurate than a true 4-SV fix.

question: How many GPS range spheres give two possible positions, one near the earth and one in space?
explanation: Two spheres intersect in a circle; a third cuts it at two points, one near the earth and one in space. A fourth is needed to remove the receiver clock error.

question: How long does each subframe of the GPS navigation message take?
explanation: Each of the five subframes takes 6 seconds, making a 30-second frame.

question: Which is the largest error source for single-frequency GPS?
explanation: Ionospheric delay (up to about 5 m single frequency) is the most significant. Others: ephemeris about 2.5 m, SV clock 1.5 m, multipath 0.6 m, receiver noise 0.3 m.

question: How does ionospheric delay depend on frequency?

options.text: It does not depend on frequency

explanation: Higher frequencies are delayed less, in proportion to 1/f². More ionization means more delay.

question: What is the approximate maximum ephemeris error?
explanation: Errors in the SV's own position, from gravitational and solar effects, are up to about 2.5 m.

question: What is the approximate maximum satellite clock error?
explanation: After the 12-hourly checks, satellite clock error contributes up to about 1.5 m.

question: How does tropospheric propagation affect GPS signals?

options.text: It reflects them back into space above the cloud tops
It has no effect at GPS frequencies

explanation: Pressure, temperature, density and humidity change the signal speed. A 1 ns timing change equals about 0.3 m of range.

question: What is the approximate maximum multipath error?
explanation: Reflections from the ground and the airframe are reduced by careful aerial siting and processing; maximum about 0.6 m. Receiver noise adds up to 0.3 m.

question: What does dilution of precision (DOP) describe?

options.text: The ionospheric delay of the signal
The weakening of the signal with range
The effect of satellite geometry on accuracy
The error in the satellite clock

explanation: The angles at which the position lines cut, together with range errors, decide how accurate the fix is. Poor geometry gives a high DOP.

question: Which DOP refers to vertical error?
explanation: HDOP: horizontal; VDOP: vertical; PDOP: both; TDOP: time; GDOP: PDOP and TDOP combined.

question: Which satellite geometry gives the best fix?

options.text: Two overhead and two on the same bearing
All four near the horizon in one direction
One overhead and three low, 120° apart

explanation: Widely spaced satellites give good cuts. The ideal is one directly overhead and three near the horizon spaced 120° apart.

question: Where is the best place for a GPS aerial on an aircraft?

options.text: On top of the fuselage, near the CG
Under the fuselage near the tail, behind the wing

explanation: Here the aircraft structure is least likely to shadow satellites in a manoeuvre or cause reflections.

question: How did Selective Availability (SA) degrade GPS?

options.text: By dithering the satellite clock time
By changing the C/A code each day
By switching satellites off at random

explanation: SA added random errors to the SV clock, reducing civil accuracy to about 100 m. It was switched off on 1 May 2000.

question: What horizontal accuracy (95%) is specified for the GPS SPS?
explanation: SPS: horizontal 13 m, vertical 22 m, time 40 ns (all 95%).

question: Why is integrity monitoring needed for GPS?

options.text: Four satellites cannot detect bad data
GPS needs a ground station to work
GPS signals fail every few minutes
GPS has no means of measuring position without a ground station

explanation: With only four SVs, a faulty satellite would go unnoticed and errors could reach hundreds of miles. Augmentation systems detect faults and warn in time.

question: What is RAIM?
explanation: RAIM is an aircraft-based augmentation (ABAS) that checks satellite data by comparing extra position solutions.

question: How many satellites does RAIM need to detect a faulty satellite?
explanation: Comparing combinations of five SVs reveals an inconsistency. To identify and exclude the faulty one and keep monitoring, six are needed.

question: Why is a minimum of six satellites recommended for RAIM?

options.text: So that a 4D fix is possible
So that two receivers can share them
So the almanac downloads faster after the receiver is switched on

explanation: With five SVs, excluding one leaves four and no further monitoring. A sixth keeps integrity monitoring available.

question: Which errors can GBAS NOT remove?
explanation: GBAS removes ephemeris and clock errors and almost cancels ionospheric and tropospheric errors near the site, but noise and multipath belong to each receiver.

question: How does a GBAS (local area augmentation) work?

options.text: A surveyed site sends corrections by VHF
The aircraft compares GPS with its IRS
An ILS is used to correct the GPS

explanation: A receiver on a precisely surveyed site compares its GPS position with the known one and sends corrections and integrity data to aircraft by a VHF data link.

question: What is a pseudolite?

options.text: A GPS receiver without a display, used for timing
A spare satellite in each plane
A satellite in a low earth orbit
A ground station acting as a satellite

explanation: A pseudolite (pseudo-satellite) at the airport transmits GNSS-type signals, here giving range to the threshold.

question: What level of approach does GBAS have the potential to support?
explanation: Near the reference site the errors are almost eliminated, giving potential for Category III operations.

question: Which of these is a satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS)?
explanation: SBAS include EGNOS (Europe), WAAS (USA), MSAS (Japan) and GAGAN (India). RAIM is aircraft-based; LAAS is ground-based.

question: At what height and period do geostationary satellites orbit?
explanation: Geostationary satellites orbit over the equator at about 35 800 km, once every 24 hours, so they stay over one point.

question: How does an SBAS reference station measure satellite errors?

options.text: It compares GPS ranges with its surveyed position
It receives errors reported by aircraft
It compares GPS with a VOR at the site
It times signals from the geostationary satellite

explanation: Knowing its exact position, the reference station works out each satellite's range error and checks integrity. These errors stay valid over hundreds of kilometres.

question: How does EGNOS correction data reach the aircraft?

options.text: Through a VHF data link at each airport

explanation: Data from reference stations goes via the master control station to an uplink, then is broadcast by geostationary satellites to suitable receivers.

question: What must be done when combining GPS and GLONASS positions?

options.text: Correct for the different speeds of light
Convert between the PZ-90 and WGS-84 models

explanation: The two systems use different earth models, so one position must be converted to the other's model before combining.

question: Which SBAS is operated by the USA?
explanation: WAAS (USA), EGNOS (Europe), MSAS (Japan), GAGAN (India). All are designed to be compatible.
